posts.title: Why I Study Ima Keithel
posts.excerpt: Ima Keithel isn't just a research site for me — it's a market I grew up hearing about, run entirely by women who have kept it running through decades of unrest. This post is about how that personal connection became a doctoral question.
posts.body:
Long before it became the subject of my doctoral thesis, Ima Keithel was simply a fact of life — a market in the heart of Imphal that has been run entirely by women for generations, through peace and through unrest alike. Growing up, I understood it the way most people from Manipur do: as an institution, not a research site.

That changed when I started reading about how conflict and digital technology were reshaping women's livelihoods elsewhere — in Kashmir, in Iraq, in the informal markets of East Java. The literature was rich, but something was missing: nobody had asked these questions here, in a market I knew, about women whose resilience I had grown up watching without naming it as such.

So the question that anchors my thesis is really quite personal: when the ground keeps shifting — politically, economically — what actually helps women vendors keep going? And where does a smartphone, a QR code, or a WhatsApp group genuinely make a difference, versus where does it fall short of what these women really need?

I don't come to this work as an outsider looking in. I come to it as someone trying to translate something I already know to be true — that these women are resilient — into research that is rigorous enough to be taken seriously, and honest enough to reflect what they actually told me.
